title: Universality of Measurement-Induced Criticality under Symmetry-Breaking Measurements
authors: Angelo Russotto, Filiberto Ares, Pasquale Calabrese
abstract: We study the critical properties of random quantum circuits with a $U(1)$ symmetry subject to local projective measurements that explicitly break this symmetry. We find that, at the measurement-induced phase transition, symmetry-breaking measurements act as a relevant perturbation at large scales, leading to the same universal critical properties as the corresponding monitored random circuit with non-symmetric unitary dynamics. In particular, we consider monitored $U(1)$-symmetric Haar-random circuits in the limit of large local Hilbert-space dimension, where the trajectory-averaged entanglement entropy can be exactly obtained in terms of a classical statistical mechanics model. In this model, the charge associated with the conservation law follows a symmetric simple exclusion process, in which symmetry-breaking measurements correspond to disordered defects that create and destroy charges. We prove that the charge correlation length remains finite for any measurement rate, ruling out a charge-sharpening transition, in contrast to the case of symmetry-preserving measurements. We further support our predictions at finite local Hilbert-space dimension through numerical finite-size scaling analyses of the entanglement transition in monitored $U(1)$-symmetric Haar and stabilizer random circuits.
summary: The paper analyzes the critical physics of quantum circuits subjected to measurements that break a global U(1) symmetry. By mapping the dynamics to a classical exclusion process in the large dimension limit, the authors prove that this symmetry breaking drives the system to a universal critical point identical to non-symmetric cases. This contrasts sharply with symmetry-preserving measurements and provides insights into how measurement protocols control quantum criticality.
main_problem: The study investigates how local projective measurements that explicitly break a global U(1) symmetry affect the critical properties of random quantum circuits.
main_result: Symmetry-breaking measurements act as relevant perturbations, driving the system to the same universal critical behavior as generic monitored circuits. Furthermore, this process prevents a charge-sharpening transition by keeping the charge correlation length finite.
method: The analysis uses the large local Hilbert-space limit ($d 	o \infty$) to map the quantum dynamics onto an exactly solvable classical statistical mechanics model (a symmetric simple exclusion process).
model_or_system: The system is a monitored random quantum circuit with U(1) symmetry, involving two-qubit gates and local projective measurements. The analysis compares this to circuits with non-symmetric unitary dynamics.
key_observables: Entanglement entropy, charge correlation length ($\xi_{charge}$), and the universality class of the Measurement-Induced Phase Transition (MIPT).
important_parameters: Measurement rate ($p$), local Hilbert-space dimension ($d 	o \infty$ limit), and the symmetry-breaking nature of the measurement operator.
main_assumptions: The primary analytical tool relies on taking the large local Hilbert-space dimension limit to map the problem onto a classical statistical model; numerical support is given for finite dimensions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 sketches the monitored random quantum circuit structure, illustrating how symmetry breaking leads to the generic MIPT universality class, while preserving symmetry leads elsewhere. Other figures detail the mapping to the SSEP and numerical scaling results.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model (U(1)-symmetric circuits with local measurements). It then analyzes the large $d$ limit by mapping entanglement entropy to a classical process. The core result proves the relevance of symmetry breaking, contrasting it with symmetry-preserving cases and providing numerical verification.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium quantum dynamics in open systems, showing how measurement back-action dictates universal critical behavior, which is highly relevant for understanding decoherence and information scrambling in physical platforms like superconducting qubits or trapped ions.
